newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania leader attacks judges over pyramid schemes.
newsitem.headline: Romania leader attacks judges over pyramid schemes.

text.p: Romania's reformist president has called for the resignation of judges he alleges got rich from a pyramid investment scheme which sank in 1994 with losses of a billion dollars.
But there was no sign that the kind of popular outrage gripping Albanian towns on Monday over the collapse of similar pyramid schemes was about to erupt in Romania.

President Emil Constantinescu, in a weekend speech to judges, denounced some who he said profited from the country's biggest get-rich-quick scheme -- "Caritas" -- which collapsed with the savings of four million Romanians.
"I can't see how a magistrate could justify his privileged position on the list of Caritas winners," he said, pressing on with an anti-corruption drive launched after his inauguration last month.
"We expect resignations...to save the honour of judges tainted by public accusations of bribe-taking, of accepting favours or undue benefits."
Romanian newspapers have in recent months published lists, apparently leaked by authorities, of up-front payments made by the Caritas scheme to public officials, including judges.
Post-communist Romania has no legal safeguards to protect investors, who know next to nothing about financial markets.
But the collapse of more than 600 dubious schemes in the first five years after the 1989 fall of communism generated only brief, subdued protests.
Authorities have put off ruling on whether to ban the schemes, which have lost their importance with the emergence of investment funds and other attractive and relatively safe savings vehicles.
"We have repeatedly recommended the adoption of a law on pyramid funds," a police spokesman told Reuters on Monday.
Police are collating complaints from millions of Romanians who lost their savings in Caritas.

The scheme's mastermind, Ioan Stoica, was freed from jail last year after a court cut his sentence on fraud charges from six to two years. His conviction was confined to misuse of public funds in the city where it was based, Cluj in Transylvania.
"Stoica was tried for defrauding the town of Cluj. He has yet to answer for the big lie -- cheating millions of depositors out of their savings," a local political analyst said.
Pyramid schemes grow by paying old depositors high returns with the deposits of new ones, but collapse when they run short of new investors.

Albanian troops were guarding government buildings in Tirana on Monday after nationwide protests and riots. Albanian President Sali Berisha has assumed additional powers to deal with the disturbances in Europe's poorest country.
"We never ruled out the possibility that such incidents could have happened here, or that they might break out at any time," said a Romanian police officer.
